The Vulgate and an ancient MS. read in the singular number, יאכל yochel, comedat, "he shall eat." "It shall be well with him:" - כי טוב ki tob, "that good." Say nothing to such but good. He is a good man, he does nothing but good, and has a good God to deal with, from whom he expects nothing but goodness. It shall be well with such in all circumstances of life. <div eID="gen26564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26565" type="x-p"/> 1. In prosperity. <div eID="gen26565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26566" type="x-p"/> 2. In adversity. <div eID="gen26566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26567" type="x-p"/> 3. In sickness. <div eID="gen26567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26568" type="x-p"/> 4. In health. <div eID="gen26568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26569" type="x-p"/> 5. In death. <div eID="gen26569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26570" type="x-p"/> 6. In judgment. And, <div eID="gen26570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26571" type="x-p"/> 7. Through eternity <div eID="gen26571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26572" type="x-p"/> In every case, occurrence, and circumstance, he shall eat the fruit of his doings - he shall derive benefit from being a righteous man, and walking in a righteous way.
entries.f487d9f5a87b6a3f56c4f1d6ac1e9872a5158078: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26573" type="x-p"/> Wo unto the wicked - לרשע lerasha, the man who is, <div eID="gen26573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26574" type="x-p"/> 1. Evil in his heart. <div eID="gen26574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26575" type="x-p"/> 2. Evil in his purposes. <div eID="gen26575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26576" type="x-p"/> 3. Evil in his life. <div eID="gen26576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26577" type="x-p"/> As he is wicked, he does that which is wicked; and is influenced by the wicked one, of whom he is the servant and the son. It shall be ill with him, רע ra; in a single word say to him - evil! Of him you can speak no good; and to him you can speak no good - all is evil, in him - before him - after him - round about him - above him - below him. Evil in time - evil through eternity! <div eID="gen26577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26578" type="x-p"/> The reward of his hands - What he has deserved he shall get. He shall be paid that for which he has labored, and his reward shall be in proportion to his work. O, what a lot is that of the wicked! Cursed in time, and accursed through eternity!
entries.10e744d54e6bdf73a432cdfacf2f48a2a72520dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen26578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26579" type="x-p"/> Err "Pervert" - בלעו billeu, "swallow." Among many unsatisfactory methods of accounting for the unusual meaning of this word in this place, I choose Jarchi's explication, as making the best sense. "Read בללו billalu, 'confound.' Syriac." - Dr. Judd. "Read בהלו beholu, 'disturb or trouble.'" - Secker. So Septuagint. This verse might be read, "The collectors of grapes shall be their oppressors; and usurers (noshim, instead of nashim, women) shall rule over them."
entries.00de597166e305f06123d8e76d255fd597d9fb37: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26580" type="x-p"/> The people "His people" - עמו ammo, Septuagint.
entries.4ddd8a54078741cb459ca8b42891f52e8f166479: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen26580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26581" type="x-p"/> The vineyard. "My vineyard" - כרמי - "dr carmi, Septuagint, Chaldee, Jerome.
entries.18fb1ecf9cf15adead33069a7e907c31356efcd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen26581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26582" type="x-p"/> And grind the faces - The expression and the image is strong, to denote grievous oppression but is exceeded by the prophet Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.1-Mic.3.3">Mic 3:1-3</reference> : - "Hear, I pray you, ye chiefs of Jacob, <div eID="gen26582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26583" type="x-p"/> And ye princes of the house of Israel: <div eID="gen26583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26584" type="x-p"/> Is it not yours to know what is right? <div eID="gen26584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26585" type="x-p"/> Ye that hate good and love evil: <div eID="gen26585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26586" type="x-p"/> Who tear their skins from off them, <div eID="gen26586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26587" type="x-p"/> And their flesh from off their bones; <div eID="gen26587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26588" type="x-p"/> Who devour the flesh of my people; <div eID="gen26588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26589" type="x-p"/> And flay from off them their skin; <div eID="gen26589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26590" type="x-p"/> And their bones they dash in pieces; <div eID="gen26590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26591" type="x-p"/> And chop them asunder, as morsels for the pot: <div eID="gen26591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26592" type="x-p"/> And as flesh thrown into the midst of the caldron." <div eID="gen26592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26593" type="x-p"/> In the last line but one, for כאשר keasher, read, by the transposition of a letter, כשאר kisher, with the Septuagint and Chaldee.
entries.8aa4a008a54f35fdebe64fc70916b375aaa32cc2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen26593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26594" type="x-p"/> And wanton eyes "And falsely setting off their eyes with paint" - Hebrew, falsifying their eyes. I take this to be the true meaning and literal rendering of the word; from שקר shakar. The Masoretes have pointed it, as if it were from שקר sakar, a different word. This arose, as I imagine, from their supposing that the word was the same with סקר sakar, Chaldee, "intueri, innuere oculis;" or that it had an affinity with the noun סיקרא sikra, which the Chaldeans, or the rabbins at least, use for stibium, the mineral which was commonly used in colouring the eyes. See Jarchi's comment on the place. Though the colouring of the eyes with stibium be not particularly here expressed, yet I suppose it to be implied; and so the Chaldee paraphrase explains it; stibio linitis oculis, "with eyes dressed with stibium." This fashion seems to have prevailed very generally among the Eastern people in ancient times; and they retain the very same to this day. <div eID="gen26594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26595" type="x-p"/> Pietro delta Valle, giving a description of his wife, an Assyrian lady born in Mesopotamia, and educated at Baghdad, whom he married in that country, (Viaggi, Tom. I., Lettera 17), says, "Her eyelashes, which are long, and, according to the custom of the East, dressed with stibium, (as we often read in the Holy Scriptures of the Hebrew women of old, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.30">Jer 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.23.40">Eze 23:40</reference>; and in Xenophon, of Astyages the grandfather of Cyrus, and of the Medes of that time, Cyropaed. lib. i.), give a dark, and at the same time a majestic, shade to the eyes." "Great eyes," says Sandys, Travels, p. 67, speaking of the Turkish women, "they have in principal repute; and of those the blacker they be the more amiable; insomuch that they put between the eyelids and the eye a certain black powder with a fine long pencil, made of a mineral, brought from the kingdom of Fez, and called Alcohole; which by the not disagreeable staining of the lids doth better set forth the whiteness of the eye; and though it be troublesome for a time, yet it comforteth the sight, and repelleth ill humours." Vis ejus (stibii) astringe ac refrigerare, principalis autem circa oculos; namque ideo etiam plerique Platyophthalmon id appellavere, quoniam in calliblepharis mulierum dilatat oculos; et fluxiones inhibet oculorum exulcerationesque. "It is astringent in its virtue, and refrigerant, and to be chiefly employed about the eyes, and it is called Platyophthalmon, for being put into those ointments with which women beautify their eyes, it dilates them, removes defluxions, and heals any ulcerations that may be about the eyelids." - Pliny, Nat. Hist. 33:6. <div eID="gen26595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26596" type="x-p"/> Ille supercilium madida fuligine tactum <div eID="gen26596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26597" type="x-p"/> Obliqua producit acu, pingitque trementes <div eID="gen26597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26598" type="x-p"/> Attollens oculos <div eID="gen26598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26599" type="x-p"/> Juv. Sat. 2:93. <div eID="gen26599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26600" type="x-p"/> One his eyebrows, tinged with black soot, <div eID="gen26600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26601" type="x-p"/> Lengthens with an oblique bodkin, and paints, <div eID="gen26601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26602" type="x-p"/> Lifting up his winking eyes. "But none of those [Moorish] ladies," says Dr. Shaw, Travels, p. 294, fol., "take themselves to be completely dressed, till they have tinged the hair and edges of their eyelids with alkahol, the powder of lead ore. This operation is performed by dipping first into the powder a small wooden bodkin of the thickness of a quill; and then drawing it afterwards through the eyelids, over the ball of the eye." Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Eze.23.40">Eze 23:40</reference>, uses the same word in the form of a verb, כחלת עניך cachalt eynayik, "thou didst dress thine eyes with alcahol;" which the Septuagint render εστιβιζου τους, οφθαλμους σου, "thou didst dress thine eyes with stibium;" just as they do when the word פוך phuch is employed: compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.30">2Kgs 9:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.30">Jer 4:30</reference>. They supposed, therefore, that פוך phuch and כחל cachal, or in the Arabic form, alcahol, meant the same thing; and probably the mineral used of old for this purpose was the same that is used now; which Dr. Shaw (ibid. note) says is "a rich lead ore, pounded into an impalpable powder." Alcoholados; the word משקרות meshakkeroth in this place is thus rendered in an old Spanish translation. - Sanctius. See also Russell's Nat. Hist. of Aleppo, p. 102. <div eID="gen26602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26603" type="x-p"/> The following inventory, as one may call it, of the wardrobe of a Hebrew lady, must, from its antiquity, and the nature of the subject, have been very obscure even to the most ancient interpreters which we have of it; and from its obscurity must have been also peculiarly liable to the mistakes of transcribers. However, it is rather matter of curiosity than of importance; and is indeed, upon the whole, more intelligible and less corrupted than one might have reasonably expected. Clemens Alexandrinus, Paedag. lib. ii., c. 12, and Julius Pollux, lib. vii., c. 22, have each of them preserved from a comedy of Aristophanes, now lost, a similar catalogue of the several parts of the dress and ornaments of a Grecian lady; which, though much more capable of illustration from other writers, though of later date, and quoted and transmitted down to us by two different authors, yet seems to be much less intelligible, and considerably more corrupted, than this passage of Isaiah. Salmasius has endeavored, by comparing the two quotations, and by much critical conjecture and learned disquisition, to restore the true reading, and to explain the particulars; with what success, I leave to the determination of the learned reader, whose curiosity shall lead him to compare the passage of the comedian with this of the prophet, and to examine the critic's learned labors upon it. Exercit. Plinian, p. 1148; or see Clem. Ales. as cited above, edit. Potter, where the passage, as corrected by Salmasius, is given. <div eID="gen26603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26604" type="x-p"/> Nich. Guel. Schroederus, professor of oriental languages in the University of Marpurg, has published a very learned and judicious treatise upon this passage of Isaiah. The title of it is, "Commentarius Philologico-Criti cus de Vestitu Mulierum Hebraearum ad Iesai 3 ver. 16-24. Lugd. Bat. 1745." As I think no one has handled this subject with so much judgment and ability as this author, I have for the most part followed him, in giving the explanation of the several terms denoting the different parts of dress, of which this passage consists; signifying the reasons of my dissent, where he does not give me full satisfaction. <div eID="gen26604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26605" type="x-p"/> Bishop Lowth's translation of these verses is the following: - <div eID="gen26605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26606" type="x-p"/> 18. In that day will the Lord take from them the ornaments,Of the feet-rings, and the net-works, and the crescents; <div eID="gen26606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26607" type="x-p"/> 19. The pendants, and the bracelets, and the veils; <div eID="gen26607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26608" type="x-p"/> 20. The tires, and the fetters, and the zones, And the perfume-boxes, and the amulets; <div eID="gen26608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26609" type="x-p"/> 21. The rings, and the jewels of the nostrils; <div eID="gen26609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26610" type="x-p"/> 22. The embroidered robes, and the tunics, And the cloaks, and the little purses, <div eID="gen26610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26611" type="x-p"/> 23. The transparent garments, and the fine linen vests, And the turbans, and the mantles. <div eID="gen26611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26612" type="x-p"/> 24. And there shall be instead of perfume, a putrid ulcer;And instead of well-girt raiment, rags;And instead of high-dressed hair, baldness;And instead of a zone, a girdle of sackcloth; And sun-burnt skin, instead of beauty. <div eID="gen26612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26613" type="x-p"/> The daughters of Zion - walk - What is meant by these several kinds of action and articles of dress cannot be well conjectured. How our ancestors understood them will appear from the following, which is the translation of these verses in my old MS. Bible: - <div eID="gen26613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26614" type="x-p"/> 16. The doughteris of Syon wenteh with strught out necks, and ib beckes (winking) of eegen, geeden and flappeden with hondis for joye, and geeden: and with theire feet in curyous goying geeden; - 17. the Lord schall fully make ballid the top of the boughtris of Syon: and the Lord the her of hem schal naken. And for ournemente schal be schenschip. <div eID="gen26614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26615" type="x-p"/> 18. In that day, the Lord schal don awey the ournement of Schoon and hoosis: 19. and beegis, and brochis, and armeerclis, and mytris; 20. and coombis, and rybanys and reversis at the hemmys, and oynment boris and ereringis; 21. and ryngis and jemmys in the frount hongynge; 22. and chaunginge clothis, and litil pallis, and scheetis, and prynys; 23. and scheweris, and neche hercheuys, and flyetis, and roketis; 24. and ther schal be for swot smel, stynke, and for gyrdil, a litl coord; and for crisp her, ballidnesse; and for brest boond and heyr. <div eID="gen26615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26616" type="x-p"/> Some of these things are hard to be understood, though I think this version as good as that of the very learned bishop: but there is little doubt that articles of clothing and dress bore these names in the fourteenth century.
entries.c83a4c1884b97cba178957fa9d00dbaa93580743: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen26616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26617" type="x-p"/> The Lord will smite "Will the Lord humble" - ταπεινωσει, Septuagint; and so Syriac and Chaldee. For שפח sippach they read שפל shaphal. Instead of יהוה Yehovah, many MSS. have אדני Adonai. <div eID="gen26617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26618" type="x-p"/> Will discover their secret parts "Expose their nakedness" - It was the barbarous custom of the conquerors of those times to strip their captives naked, and to make them travel in that condition, exposed to the inclemency of the weather; and the worst of all, to the intolerable heat of the sun. But this to the women was the height of cruelty and indignity; and especially to such as those here described, who had indulged themselves in all manner of delicacies of living, and all the superfluities of ornamental dress; and even whose faces had hardly ever been exposed to the sight of man. This is always mentioned as the hardest part of the lot of captives. Nahum, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Nah 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Nah.3.6">Nah 3:6</reference>, denouncing the fate of Nineveh, paints it in very strong colors: - "Behold, I am against thee, saith Jehovah, God of hosts: <div eID="gen26618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26619" type="x-p"/> And I will discover thy skirts upon thy face; <div eID="gen26619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26620" type="x-p"/> And I will expose thy nakedness to the nations; <div eID="gen26620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26621" type="x-p"/> And to the kingdoms thy shame. <div eID="gen26621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26622" type="x-p"/> And I will throw ordures upon thee; <div eID="gen26622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26623" type="x-p"/> And I will make thee vile, and set thee as a gazing-stock."
entries.8f921baf539f2012e28920628c8dd9884c389f26: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen26623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26624" type="x-p"/> Ornaments about their feet "The ornaments of the feet rings" - The late learned Dr. Hunt, professor of Hebrew and Arabic in the University of Oxford, has very well explained the word עכס both verb and noun, in his very ingenious Dissertation on Prov, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.22">Isa 7:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.23">Isa 7:23</reference>. The verb means to skip, to bound, to dance along, and the noun, those ornaments of the feet which the Eastern ladies wore; chains or rings, which made a tinkling sound as they moved nimbly in walking. Eugene Roger, Description de la Terre Sainte, 54:2 ch. 2, speaking of the Arabian women, of the first rank in Palestine, says,"Au lieu de brasselets elles ont de menottes d'argent, qu'elles portent aux poignets et aux pieds; ou sont attachez quantite de petits annelets d'argent, qui font un cliquetis comme d'une cymbale, lorsqu'elles cheminent ou se mouvent quelque peu." See Dr. Hunt's Dissertation; where he produces other testimonies to the same purpose from authors of travels. Hindoo women of ill fame wear loose ornaments one above another on their ankles, which at every motion make a tinkling noise. See Ward. <div eID="gen26624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26625" type="x-p"/> And their cauls "the net-works" - I am obliged to differ from the learned Schroederus almost at first setting out. He renders the word שביסים shebisim by soliculi, little ornaments, bullae, or studs, in shape representing the sun, and so answering to the following word שהרנים saharonim, lunulae, crescents. He supposes the word to be the same with שמישים shemishim, the י yod in the second syllable making the word diminutive, and the letter מ mem being changed for ב beth, a letter of the same organ. How just and well founded his authorities for the transmutation of these letters in the Arabic language are, I cannot pretend to judge; but as I know of no such instance in Hebrew, it seems to me a very forced etymology. Being dissatisfied with this account of the matter, I applied to my good friend above mentioned, the late Dr. Hunt, who very kindly returned the following answer to my inquiries: - "I have consulted the Arabic Lexicons, as well MS. as printed, but cannot find שביסים shebisim in any of them, nor any thing belonging to it; so that no help is to be had from that language towards clearing up the meaning of this difficult word. But what the Arabic denies, the Syriac perhaps may afford; in which I find the verb שבש shabas, to entangle or interweave, an etymology which is equally favorable to our marginal translation, net-works, with שבץ shabats, to make chequer work, or embroider, (the word by which Kimchi and others have explained שביס shabis); and has moreover this advantage over it, that the letters ש sin and ס samech are very frequently put for each other, but צ tsaddi and ס samech scarcely ever. Aben Ezra joins שביסים shebisim and עכסים achasim, which immediately precedes it, together; and says that שביס shabis was the ornament of the leps, as עכס eches was of the feet. His words are, שביס תכשיט של שוקים כמו עכס של רגלים - L."
entries.bc60706060b240b541d64f034c381a00624a6b1b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen26625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26626" type="x-p"/> The tablets - The words בתי הנפש bottey hannephesh, which we translate tablets, and Bishop Lowth, perfume boxes, literally signify houses of the soul; and may refer to strong scented bottles used for pleasure and against fainting; similar to bottles with otto of roses, worn by the ladies of the East to the present time.
entries.95e188036ed960d1db93c4991743817b101a4463: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen26626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26627" type="x-p"/> Nose-jewels "The jewels of the nostril" - נזמי האף nizmey haaph. Schroederus explains this, as many others do, of jewels, or strings of pearl hanging from the forehead, and reaching to the upper part of the nose; than which nothing can be more ridiculous, as such are seldom seen on an Asiatic face. But it appears from many passages of Holy Scripture that the phrase is to be literally and properly understood of nose-jewels, rings set with jewels hanging from the nostrils, as ear-rings from the ears, by holes bored to receive them. <div eID="gen26627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26628" type="x-p"/> Ezekiel, enumerating the common ornaments of women of the first rank, has not omitted this particular, and is to be understood in the same manner, <reference osisRef="Eze.16.11">Eze 16:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.16.12">Eze 16:12</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Gen.24.47">Gen 24:47</reference> : - "And I decked thee with ornaments; <div eID="gen26628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26629" type="x-p"/> And I put bracelets upon thine hands, <div eID="gen26629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26630" type="x-p"/> And a chain on thy neck: <div eID="gen26630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26631" type="x-p"/> And I put a jewel on thy nose, <div eID="gen26631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26632" type="x-p"/> And ear-rings on thine ears, <div eID="gen26632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26633" type="x-p"/> And a splendid crown upon thine head." <div eID="gen26633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26634" type="x-p"/> And in an elegant proverb of Solomon, <reference osisRef="Pro.11.22">Pro 11:22</reference>, there is a manifest allusion to this kind of ornament, which shows it to have been used in his time: - "As a jewel of gold in the snout of a swine; <div eID="gen26634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26635" type="x-p"/> So is a woman beautiful, but wanting discretion." <div eID="gen26635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26636" type="x-p"/> This fashion, however strange it may appear to us, was formerly and is still common in many parts of the East, among women of all ranks. Paul Lucas, speaking of a village or clan of wandering people, a little on this side of the Euphrates, says, (2d Voyage du Levant, tom. i., art. 24), "The women, almost all of them, travel on foot; I saw none handsome among them. They have almost all of them the nose bored; and wear in it a great ring, which makes them still more deformed." But in regard to this custom, better authority cannot be produced than that of Pietro della Valle, in the account which he gives of the lady before mentioned, Signora Maani Gioerida, his own wife. The description of her dress, as to the ornamental parts of it, with which he introduces the mention of this particular, will give us some notion of the taste of the Eastern ladies for finery. "The ornaments of gold and of jewels for the head, for the neck, for the arms, for the legs, and for the feet (for they wear rings even on their toes) are indeed, unlike those of the Turks, carried to great excess, but not of great value: for in Bagdad jewels of high price are either not to be had, or are not used; and they wear such only as are of little value, as turquoises, small rubies, emeralds, carbuncles, garnets, pearls, and the like. My spouse dresses herself with all of them according to their fashion; with exception, however, of certain ugly rings of very large size, set with jewels, which, in truth, very absurdly, it is the custom to wear fastened to one of their nostrils, like buffaloes: an ancient custom, however, in the East, which, as we find in the Holy Scriptures, prevailed among the Hebrew ladies even in the time of Solomon, <reference osisRef="Pro.11.22">Pro 11:22</reference>. These nose-rings, in complaisance to me, she has left off, but I have not yet been able to prevail with her cousin and her sisters to do the same; so fond are they of an old custom, be it ever so absurd, who have been long habituated to it." Viaggi, Tom. i., Let. 17. <div eID="gen26636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26637" type="x-p"/> It is the left nostril that is bored and ornamented with rings and jewels. More than one hundred drawings from life of Eastern ladies lie now before me, and scarcely one is without the nose-jewel: both the arms and wrists are covered with bracelets, arm-circles, etc., as also their legs and feet; the soles of their feet and palms of their hands coloured beautifully red with henna, and their hair plaited and ornamented superbly. These beautiful drawings are a fine comment on this chapter.
entries.df74ad2a269302e7ecd9bf99969cb9e16fa8e45b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen26637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26638" type="x-p"/> The glasses - The conjunction ו vau, and - And the glasses, is added here by forty-three of Kennicott's and thirty-four of De Rossi's MSS., and one of my own, ancient, as well as by many editions. <div eID="gen26638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26639" type="x-p"/> And the veils. "The transparent garments" - Τα διαφανη Λακωνικα, Sept. A kind of silken dress, transparent, like gauze; worn only by the most elegant women, and such as dressed themselves elegantius quam necesse esset probis, "more elegantly than modest women should." Such garments are worn to the present day; garments that not only show the shape of every part of the body, but the very color of the skin. This is evidently the case in some scores of drawings of Asiatic females now before me. This sort of garments was afterwards in use among the Greeks. Prodicus, in his celebrated fable (Xenoph. Memorab. Socr. lib. ii.) exhibits the personage of Sloth in this dress: Εσθητα δε, εξ ἡς αν μαλιστα ὡρα διαλαμποι: - "Her robe betray'd <div eID="gen26639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26640" type="x-p"/> Through the clear texture every tender limb, <div eID="gen26640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26641" type="x-p"/> Height'ning the charms it only seem'd to shade; <div eID="gen26641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26642" type="x-p"/> And as it flow'd adown so loose and thin, <div eID="gen26642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26643" type="x-p"/> Her stature show'd more tall, more snowy white her skin." <div eID="gen26643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26644" type="x-p"/> They were called multitia and coa (scil, vestimenta) by the Romans, from their being invented, or rather introduced into Greece, by one Pamphila of the island of Cos. This, like other Grecian fashions, was received at Rome, when luxury began to prevail under the emperors. It was sometimes worn even by the men, but looked upon as a mark of extreme effeminacy. See Juvenal, Sat. ii., 65, etc. Publius Syrus, who lived when the fashion was first introduced, has given a humorous satirical description of it in two lines, which by chance have been preserved: - "Aequum est, induere nuptam ventum textilem? <div eID="gen26644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26645" type="x-p"/> Palam prostare nudam in nebula linea?"
entries.f8a52585ded2838f29cffebcd17d64ad3f0a419c: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen26645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26646" type="x-p"/> Instead of sweet smell "perfume" - A principal part of the delicacy of the Asiatic ladies consists in the use of baths, and of the richest oils and perfumes; an attention to which is in some degree necessary in those hot countries. Frequent mention is made of the rich ointments of the spouse in the Song of Solomon, <reference osisRef="Sol.4.10">Sol 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Sol.4.11">Sol 4:11</reference> : - "How beautiful are thy breasts, my sister, my spouse! <div eID="gen26646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26647" type="x-p"/> How much more excellent than wine; <div eID="gen26647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26648" type="x-p"/> And the odour of thine ointments than all perfumes! <div eID="gen26648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26649" type="x-p"/> Thy lips drop as the honey-comb, my spouse! <div eID="gen26649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26650" type="x-p"/> Honey and milk are under thy tongue: <div eID="gen26650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26651" type="x-p"/> And the odor of thy garments is as the odour of Lebanon." <div eID="gen26651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26652" type="x-p"/> The preparation for Esther's being introduced to King Ahasuerus was a course of bathing and perfuming for a whole year; "six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours;" <reference osisRef="Est.2.12">Est 2:12</reference> (note). A diseased and loathsome habit of body, instead of a beautiful skin, softened and made agreeable with all that art could devise, and all that nature, so prodigal in those countries of the richest perfumes, could supply, must have been a punishment the most severe and the most mortifying to the delicacy of these haughty daughters of Sion. <div eID="gen26652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26653" type="x-p"/> Burning instead of beauty "A sunburnt skin" - Gaspar Sanctius thinks the words כי תחת ki thachath an interpolation, because the Vulgate has omitted them. The clause כי תחת יפי ki thachath yophi seems to me rather to be imperfect at the end. Not to mention that כי ki, taken as a noun for adustio, burning, is without example, and very improbable. The passage ends abruptly, and seems to want a fuller conclusion. <div eID="gen26653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26654" type="x-p"/> In agreement with which opinion, of the defect of the Hebrew text in this place, the Septuagint, according to MSS. Pachom. and 1 D. ii., and Marchal., which are of the best authority, express it with the same evident marks of imperfection at the end of the sentence; thus: ταυτα σοι αντι καλλωπισμου The two latter add δου. This chasm in the text, from the loss probably of three or four words, seems therefore to be of long standing. <div eID="gen26654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26655" type="x-p"/> Taking כי ki in its usual sense, as a particle, and supplying לך lech from the σοι of the Septuagint, it might possibly have been originally somewhat in this form: - מראה רעת לך תהיה יפי תחת כי marah raath lech thihyeh yophi thachath ki "Yea, instead of beauty thou shalt have an illfavoured countenance." כי תחת יפי ki thachath yophi (q. יחת yachath), "for beauty shall be destroyed." Syr. חתת chathath or נחת nachath.-Dr. Durell. "May it not be כהי cohey, 'wrinkles instead of beauty?' as from יפה yaphah is formed יפי yephi, yophi; from מרה marah, מרי meri, etc.; so from כהה cahah, to be wrinkled, כהי cohey." - Dr. Jubb. The כי ki is wanting in one MS., and has been omitted by several of the ancients.
entries.7235c3289194bcde984b7c7bdfe80dc1dfe64800: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen26655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26656" type="x-p"/> Thy mighty men - For גבורתך geburathech an ancient MS. has גבורך gibborech. The true reading, from the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Chaldee, seems to be גבוריך gibborayich.
entries.11587279db99739e934700241b3c5721fb9811be: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen26656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26657" type="x-p"/> Sit upon the ground - Sitting on the ground was a posture that denoted mourning and deep distress. The prophet Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.8">Lam 2:8</reference>) has given it the first place among many indications of sorrow, in the following elegant description of the same state of distress of his country: - "The elders of the daughter of Sion sit on the ground, they are silent: They have cast up dust on their heads; they have girded themselves with sackcloth; The virgins of Jerusalem have bowed down their heads to the ground." "We find Judea," says Mr. Addison, (on Medals, Dial. ii), "on several coins of Vespasian and Titus, in a posture that denotes sorrow and captivity. I need not mention her sitting on the ground, because we have already spoken of the aptness of such a posture to represent an extreme affliction. I fancy the Romans might have an eye on the customs of the Jewish nation, as well as those of their country, in the several marks of sorrow they have set on this figure. The psalmist describes the Jews lamenting their captivity in the same pensive posture: 'By the waters of Babylon we sat down and wept, when we remembered thee, O Zion.' But what is more remarkable, we find Judea represented as a woman in sorrow sitting on the ground, in a passage of the prophet, that foretells the very captivity recorded on this medal." Mr. Addison, I presume, refers to this place of Isaiah; and therefore must have understood it as foretelling the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation by the Romans: whereas it seems plainly to relate, in its first and more immediate view at least, to the destruction of the city by Nebuchadnezzar, and the dissolution of the Jewish state under the captivity at Babylon. - L. <div eID="gen26657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26658" type="x-p"/> Several of the coins mentioned here by Mr. Addison are in my own collection: and to such I have already referred in this work. I shall describe one here. On the obverse a fine head of the emperor Vespasian with this legend, Imperator Julius Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, Tribunitia Potestate Pater Patriae, Consul VIII. <div eID="gen26658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26659" type="x-p"/> On the reverse a tall palm tree, emblem of the land of Palestine, the emperor standing on the left, close to the tree, with a trophy behind him; on the right, Judea under the figure of a female captive sitting on the ground, with her head resting on her hand, the elbow on her knee, weeping. Around is this legend, Judea Capta. Senates Consulto. However this prediction may refer proximately to the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, I am fully of opinion that it ultimately refers to the final ruin of the Jewish state by the Romans. And so it has been understood by the general run of the best and most learned interpreters and critics.  <chapter eID="Isa.3"/> <div eID="gen26659" type="x-p"/>

entries.c88468a0a6e07174bdb272bd3426772406c1d284: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“For, behold, the Lord, Jehovah of hosts, takes away from Jerusalem and from Judah supporter and means of support, every support of bread and every support of water.”</hi> The divine name given here, “The Lord, Jehovah of hosts,” with which Isaiah everywhere introduces the judicial acts of God (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Isa 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33">Isa 10:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">Isa 19:4</reference>), is a proof that the proclamation of judgment commences afresh here. Trusting in man was the crying sin, more especially of the times of Uzziah-Jotham. The glory of the kingdom at that time carried the wrath of Jehovah within it. The outbreak of that wrath commenced in the time of Ahaz; and even under Hezekiah it was merely suspended, not changed. Isaiah foretells this outbreak of wrath. He describes how Jehovah will lay the Jewish state in ruins, by taking away the main supports of its existence and growth. “Supporter and means of support” (<hi type="italic">mash'en</hi> and <hi type="italic">mash'enah</hi>) express, first of all, the general idea. The two nouns, which are only the masculine and feminine forms of one and the same word (compare Mic 2:4; <reference osisRef="Nah.2.11">Nah 2:11</reference>, and the examples from the Syriac and Arabic in Ewald, §172, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), serve to complete the generalization: <hi type="italic">fulcra omne genus</hi> (props of every kind, <hi type="italic">omnigena</hi>). They are both technical terms, denoting the prop which a person uses to support anything, whilst <hi type="italic">mish'an</hi> signifies that which yields support; so that the three correspond somewhat to the Latin <hi type="italic">fulcrum</hi>, <hi type="italic">fultura</hi>, <hi type="italic">fulcimen</hi>. Of the various means of support, bread and wine are mentioned first, not in a figurative sense, but as the two indispensable conditions and the lowest basis of human life. Life is supported by bread and water: it walks, as it were, upon the crutch of bread, so that “breaking the staff of bread” (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.26">Lev 26:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.4.16">Eze 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.16">Eze 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.13">Eze 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.16">Psa 105:16</reference>) is equivalent to physical destruction. The destruction of the Jewish state would accordingly be commenced by a removal on the part of Jehovah of all the support afforded by bread and water, i.e., all the stores of both. And this was literally fulfilled, for both in the Chaldean and Roman times Jerusalem perished in the midst of just such terrible famines as are threatened in the curses in Lev 26, and more especially in Deut 28; ; and in both cases the inhabitants were reduced to such extremities, that women devoured their own children (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.20">Lam 2:20</reference>; Josephus, <hi type="italic">Wars of Jews</hi>, vi. 3, 3, 4). It is very unjust, therefore, on the part of modern critics, such as Hitzig, Knobel, and Meier, to pronounce <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference></hi> a gloss, and, in fact, a false one. Gesenius and Umbreit retracted this suspicion. The construction of the v. is just the same as that of <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference>; and it is Isaiah’s custom to explain his own figures, as we have already observed when comparing Isa 1:7. and <reference osisRef="Isa.1.23">Isa 1:23</reference> with what preceded them. “Every support of bread and every support of water” are not to be regarded in this case as an explanation of the general idea introduced before, “supporters and means of support,” but simply as the commencement of the detailed expansion of the idea. For the enumeration of the supports which Jehovah would take away is continued in the next two verses.
entries.7749bcf830f45dd85c6f7fa24074f7ce621fdbb7: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.2-Isa.3.3">Isa 3:2-3</reference> <hi type="italic">“Hero and man of war, judge and prophet, and soothsayer and elder; captains of fifty, and the highly distinguished, and counsellors, and masters in art, and those skilled in muttering.”</hi> As the state had grown into a military state under Uzziah-Jotham, the prophet commences in both vv. with military officers, viz., the <hi type="italic">gibbor</hi>, i.e., commanders whose bravery had been already tried; the <hi type="italic">“man of war”</hi> (<hi type="italic">ish</hi> <hi type="italic">imlchâmâh</hi>), i.e., private soldiers who had been equipped and well trained (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.20">Eze 39:20</reference>); and the “captain of fifty” (<hi type="italic">sar</hi> <hi type="italic">Chamisshim</hi>), leaders of the smallest divisions of the army, consisting of only fifty men (<hi type="italic">pentekontarchos</hi>, 2Ki 1:9, etc.). The prominent members of the state are all mixed up together; <hi type="italic">“the judge”</hi> (<hi type="italic">shophet</hi>), i.e., the officers appointed by the government to administer justice; <hi type="italic">“the elder”</hi> (<hi type="italic">zâkēn</hi>), i.e., the heads of families and the senators appointed by the town corporations; the <hi type="italic">“counsellor”</hi> (<hi type="italic">yōetz</hi>), those nearest to the king; the <hi type="italic">“highly distinguished”</hi> (<hi type="italic">nesu</hi> <hi type="italic">panim</hi>), lit., those whose personal appearance (<hi type="italic">panim</hi>) was accepted, i.e., welcome and regarded with honour (Saad.: <hi type="italic">wa'gı̄h</hi>, from <hi type="italic">wa'gh</hi>, the face of appearance), that is to say, persons of influence, not only on account of their office, but also on account of wealth, age, goodness, etc.; <hi type="italic">“masters in art”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Chacam</hi> <hi type="italic">Charâshim</hi>: lxx σοφὸς ἀρχιτέκτων ), or, as Jerome has very well rendered it, <hi type="italic">in artibus mechanicis exercitatus easque callide tractans</hi> (persons well versed in mechanical arts, and carrying them out with skill). In the Chaldean captivities skilled artisans are particularly mentioned as having been carried away (2Ki 24:14.; <reference osisRef="Jer.24.1">Jer 24:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.2">Jer 29:2</reference>); so that there can be no doubt whatever that <hi type="italic">Charâshim</hi> (from <hi type="italic">Cheresh</hi>) is to be understood as signifying <hi type="italic">mechanical</hi> and not <hi type="italic">magical</hi> arts, as Gesenius, Hitzig, and Meier suppose, and therefore that <hi type="italic">Chacam</hi> <hi type="italic">Charâshim</hi> does not mean “wizards,” as Ewald renders it (<hi type="italic">Chărâshim</hi> is a different word from <hi type="italic">Chârâshim</hi>, <hi type="italic">fabri</hi>, from <hi type="italic">Chârâsh</hi>, although in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.14">1Ch 4:14</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Neh.11.35">Neh 11:35</reference>, the word is regularly pointed חרשׁים even in this personal sense). Moreover, the rendering “wizards” produces tautology, inasmuch as masters of the black art are cited as <hi type="italic">nebon</hi> <hi type="italic">lachash</hi>, “skilled in muttering.” <hi type="italic">Lachash</hi> is the whispering or muttering of magical formulas; it is related both radically and in meaning to <hi type="italic">nachash</hi>, enchantment (Arabic <hi type="italic">nachs</hi>, misfortune); it is derived from <hi type="italic">lachash</hi>, <hi type="italic">sibilare</hi>, to hiss (a kindred word to <hi type="italic">nâchash</hi>; hence <hi type="italic">nâchâsh</hi>, a serpent). Beside this, the masters of the black art are also represented as <hi type="italic">kosem</hi>, which, in accordance with the radical idea of making fast, swearing, conjuring, denoted a soothsayer following heathen superstitions, as distinguished from the <hi type="italic">nabi</hi>, of false Jehovah prophet (we find this as early as <reference osisRef="Deut.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.14">Deu 18:14</reference>).<note placement="foot">According to the primary meaning of the whole <hi type="italic">thema</hi>, which is one of hardness, rigidity, firmness, <hi type="italic">aksama</hi> (<hi type="italic">hi</hi>. of <hi type="italic">kâsam</hi>) signifies, strictly speaking, to <hi type="italic">make sure</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">to swear</hi>, either by swearing to the truth and certainty of a thing, or by making a person swear that he will do or not do a certain thing, by laying as it were a <hi type="italic">kasam</hi> upon him. The <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, on the other hand (<hi type="italic">kasama</hi>), gets its meaning to divide from the turn given to the radical idea in the substantive <hi type="italic">kism</hi>, which signifies, according to the original lexicographers, something fixed (= <hi type="italic">nası̄b</hi>), definite, i.e., a definite portion. There is just the same association of ideas in <hi type="italic">‛azama</hi> as in <hi type="italic">aksama</hi>, namely, literally to be firm or make firm, i.e., to direct one’s will firmly towards an object or place; also to direct one’s will firmly towards a person, to adjure him to do a thing or not to do it; sometimes with a softer meaning, to urge or invite a person to anything, at other times to recite conjuring formulas (<hi type="italic">‛azâim</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen12828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12829" type="x-p"/> These came next to bread and water, and were in a higher grade the props of the state. They are mixed together in this manner without regular order, because the powerful and splendid state was really a <hi type="italic">quodlibet</hi> of things Jewish and heathen; and when the wrath of Jehovah broke out, the godless glory would soon become a mass of confusion.
entries.35ecd238c92e092e4da7e54b19e397fdf04464b6: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.4">Isa 3:4</reference> <div eID="gen12829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12830" type="x-p"/> Thus robbed of its support, and torn out of its proper groove, the kingdom of Judah would fall a prey to the most shameless despotism: <hi type="italic">“And I give them boys for princes, and caprices shall rule over them.”</hi> The revived “Solomonian” glory is followed, as before, by the times of Rehoboam. The king is not expressly named. This was intentional. He had sunk into the mere shadow of a king: it was not he who ruled, but the aristocratic party that surrounded him, who led him about in leading strings as <hi type="italic">unum inter pares</hi>. Now, if it is a misfortune in most cases for a king to be a child (<hi type="italic">na'ar</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ecc 10:16</reference>), the misfortune is twice as great when the princes or magnates who surround and advise him are youngsters (<hi type="italic">ne'ârim</hi>, i.e., young lords) in a bad sense. It produces a government of <hi type="italic">tâlulim</hi>. None of the nouns in this form have a personal signification. According to the primary meaning of the verbal stem, the word might signify childishnesses, equivalent to little children (the abstract for the concrete, like τἀπαιδικά <hi type="italic">amasius</hi>), as Ewald supposes; or puppets, <hi type="italic">fantocci</hi>, poltroons, or men without heart or brain, as Luzzatto maintains. But the latter has no support in the general usage of the language, and the verb <hi type="italic">yimshelu</hi> (shall rule) does not necessarily require a personal subject (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.19.14">Psa 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.19">Psa 103:19</reference>). The word <hi type="italic">tâlulim</hi> is formed from the reflective verb <hi type="italic">hithallel</hi>, which means to meddle, to gratify one’s self, to indulge one’s caprice. Accordingly <hi type="italic">tâlulim</hi> itself might be rendered <hi type="italic">vexationes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.4">Isa 66:4</reference>). Jerome, who translates the word <hi type="italic">effeminati</hi>, appears to have thought of התעלּל in an erotic sense. The Sept. rendering, ἐμπαῖκται is better, though ἐμπαίγματα would be more exact. When used, as the word is here, along with <hi type="italic">ne'arim</hi>, it signifies outbursts of youthful caprice, which do injury to others, whether in joke or earnest. Neither law nor justice would rule, but the very opposite of justice: a course of conduct which would make subjects, like slaves, the helpless victims at one time of their lust (Jdg 19:25), and at another of their cruelty. They would be governed by lawless and bloodstained caprice, of the most despotic character and varied forms. And the people would resemble their rulers: their passions would be let loose, and all restraints of modesty and decorum be snapt asunder.
entries.47ffcfa4c2776fc5bda7d87c8a83bc20a458f628: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5">Isa 3:5</reference> <hi type="italic">“And the people oppress one another, one this and another that; the boy breaks out violently upon the old man, and the despised upon the honoured.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Niggas</hi> is the reciprocal <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, as the clause depicting the reciprocity clearly shows (cf., <hi type="italic">nilcham</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.2">Isa 19:2</reference>); <hi type="italic">nagas</hi> followed by <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> means to treat as a tyrant or taskmaster (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Isa 9:3</reference>). The commonest selfishness would then stifle every nobler motive; one would become the tyrant of another, and ill-mannered insolence would take the place of that reverence, which is due to the old and esteemed from boys and those who are below them in position, whether we regard the law of nature, the Mosaic law (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Lev 19:32</reference>), or the common custom of society. <hi type="italic">Nikleh</hi> (from <hi type="italic">kâlâh</hi>, the synonym of הקל, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.9">Isa 23:9</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa 16:14</reference>, <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, to be light or insignificant) was a term used to denote whoever belonged to the lowest stratum of society (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.23">1Sa 18:23</reference>). It was the opposite of <hi type="italic">nichâd</hi> (from <hi type="italic">Cabed</hi>, to be heavy or of great importance). The Septuagint rendering, ὁ ἄτιμος πρὸς τὸν ἔντιμον is a very good one (as the Semitic languages have no such antithetical formations with ἃ στερητικόν). With such contempt of the distinctions arising from age and position, the state would very soon become a scene of the wildest confusion.
entries.5d69d236f17d7d27078b7570524b47ba73364a30: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.6-Isa.3.7">Isa 3:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen12830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12831" type="x-p"/> At length there would be no authorities left; even the desire to rule would die out: for despotism is sure to be followed by mob-rule, and mob-rule by anarchy in the most literal sense. The distress would become so great, that whoever had a coat (cloak), so as to be able to clothe himself at all decently, would be asked to undertake the government. <hi type="italic">“When a man shall take hold of his brother in his father’s house, Thou hast a coat, thou shalt be our ruler, and take this ruin under thy hand; he will cry out in that day, I do not want to be a surgeon; there is neither bread nor coat in my house: ye cannot make me the ruler of the people.”</hi> <hi type="italic">“his father’s house”</hi> - this is not an unmeaning trait in the picture of misery. The population would have become so thin and dispirited through hunger, that with a little energy it would be possible to decide within the narrow circle of a family who should be ruler, and to give effect to the decision. “In his father’s house:” <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">âbiv</hi> is an <hi type="italic">acc. loci</hi>. The father’s house is the place where brother meets with brother; and one breaks out with the urgent petition contained in the words, which follow without the introductory “saying” (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.14.8">Isa 14:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.16">Isa 14:16</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.22.16">Isa 22:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.14">Isa 33:14</reference>). לכה for לך with <hi type="italic">He</hi> <hi type="italic">otians</hi>, a form rarely met with (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.27.37">Gen 27:37</reference>). תּהיה, which would be written תּהי before the predicate, is jussive in meaning, though not in form. <hi type="italic">“This ruin:”</hi> <hi type="italic">macshelah</hi> is used in Zep 1:3 for that which occasions a person’s fall; here it signifies what has been overthrown; and as <hi type="italic">Câshal</hi> itself, which means not only to stumble, strip, or slide, but also to fall in consequence of some force applied from without, is not used in connection with falling buildings, it must be introduced here with an allusion to the prosopopeia which follows in Isa 3:8. The man who was distinguished above all others, or at any rate above many others, by the fact that he could still dress himself decently (even if it were only in a blouse), should be made supreme ruler or dictator (cf., <hi type="italic">kâtzin</hi>, Jdg 11:6); and the state which lay so miserably in ruins should be under his hand, i.e., his direction, protection, and care (2Ki 8:20; <reference osisRef="Gen.41.35">Gen 41:35</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>, where the plural is used instead of the ordinary singular <hi type="italic">yâd</hi>.) The apodosis to the protasis introduced with <hi type="italic">Chi</hi> as a particle of time (<hi type="italic">when</hi>) commences in Isa 3:7. The answer given by the brother to the earnest petition is introduced with <hi type="italic">“he will raise</hi> (viz., his voice, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.14">Isa 24:14</reference>) <hi type="italic">in that day, saying.”</hi> It is given in this circumstantial manner because it is a solemn protest. He does not want to be a <hi type="italic">Chobēsh</hi>, i.e., a <hi type="italic">binder</hi>, namely of the broken arms, and bones, and ribs of the ruined state (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa 30:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa 61:1</reference>). The expression <hi type="italic">ehyeh</hi> implies that he does not like it, because he is conscious of his inability. He has not confidence enough in himself, and the assumption that he has a coat is a false cone: he not only has no coat at home (we must remember that the conversation is supposed to take place in his father’s house), but he has not any bread; so that it is utterly impossible for a naked, starving man like him to do what is suggested (“in my house,” <hi type="italic">ubebethi</hi> with a <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> of causal connection: Ges. 155, 1, <hi type="italic">c</hi>).
entries.884cb6670482335c1c6f19b525663989e4582efe: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.8">Isa 3:8</reference> <div eID="gen12831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12832" type="x-p"/> The prophet then proceeds, in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.8-Isa.3.12">Isa 3:8-12</reference>, to describe this deep, tragical misery as a just retribution.<hi type="italic">”For Jerusalem is ruined and Judah fallen; because their tongue and their doings </hi>(are)<hi type="italic">against Jehovah, to defy the eyes of His glory.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Jerusalem</hi> as a city is feminine, according to the usual personification; <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> as a people is regarded as masculine.<note placement="foot">As a rule, the name of a people (apart from the personification of the people as <hi type="italic">beth</hi>, a house) is only used as a feminine, when the name of the land stands for the nation itself (see Gesenius, <hi type="italic">Lehrbegr.</hi> p. 469).</note> <div eID="gen12832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12833" type="x-p"/> The two preterites <hi type="italic">Câs'lah</hi> and <hi type="italic">nâphal</hi> express the general fact, which occasioned such scenes of misery as the one just described. The second clause, beginning with “because” (<hi type="italic">Chi</hi>), is a substantive clause, and attributes the coming judgment not to future sin, but to sin already existing. <hi type="italic">“Again Jehovah:”</hi> אל is used to denote a hostile attitude, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Isa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.8">Gen 4:8</reference>; Num 32:14; Jos 10:6. The capital and the land are against Jehovah both in word and deed, “to defy the eyes of His glory” (<hi type="italic">lamroth</hi> <hi type="italic">‛ēnē</hi> <hi type="italic">Chebodo</hi>). עני is equivalent to עיני; and <hi type="italic">lamroth</hi> is a syncopated <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.23.11">Isa 23:11</reference>, and like the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.12">Isa 1:12</reference> : we find the same form of the same word in Psa 78:17. The <hi type="italic">kal</hi> <hi type="italic">mârâh</hi>, which is also frequently construed with the accusative, signifies to thrust away in a refractory manner; the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> <hi type="italic">himrâh</hi>, to treat refractorily, literally to set one’s self rigidly in opposition, <hi type="italic">obniti</hi>; <hi type="italic">mar</hi>, <hi type="italic">stringere</hi>, to draw tightly, with which unquestionably the meaning bitter as an astringent is connected, though it does not follow that <hi type="italic">mârâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">himrâh</hi>, and <hi type="italic">hemar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">Exo 23:21</reference>) can be rendered παραπικραίνειν, as they have been in the Septuagint, since the idea of opposing, resisting, fighting in opposition, is implied in all these roots, with distinct reference to the primary meaning. The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> is a shorter expression instead of למען, which is the term generally employed in such circumstances (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amo 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.18">Jer 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">Jer 32:29</reference>). But what does the prophet mean by “the eyes of His glory?” Knobel’s assertion, that <hi type="italic">Châbod</hi> is used here for the religious glory, i.e., the holiness of God, is a very strange one, since the <hi type="italic">Châbod</hi> of God is invariably the fiery, bright <hi type="italic">doxa</hi> which reveals Him as the Holy One. but his remark does not meet the question, inasmuch as it does not settle the point in dispute, whether the expression “the eyes of His glory” implies that the glory itself has eyes, or the glory is a quality of the eyes. The construction is certainly not a different one from “the arm of His glory” in <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">Isa 52:10</reference>, so that it is to be taken as an attribute. But this suggests the further question, what does the prophet mean by the glory-eyes or glorious eyes of Jehovah? If we were to say the eyes of Jehovah are His knowledge of the world, it would be impossible to understand how they could be called holy, still less how they could be called glorious. This abstract explanation of the anthropomorphisms cannot be sustained. The state of the case is rather the following. The glory (<hi type="italic">Châbod</hi>) of God is that eternal and glorious <hi type="italic">morphē</hi> which His holy nature assumes, and which men must picture to themselves anthropomorphically, because they cannot imagine anything superior to the human form. In this glorious form Jehovah looks upon His people with eyes of glory. His pure but yet jealous love, His holy love which breaks out in wrath against all who meet it with hatred instead of with love, is reflected therein.
entries.1f6d4f5edf1a0c6401c39648b2254ae3bf7695fb: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.9">Isa 3:9</reference> <div eID="gen12833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12834" type="x-p"/> But Israel, instead of walking in the consciousness of being a constant and favourite object of these majestic, earnestly admonishing eyes, was diligently engaged in bidding them defiance both in word and deed, not even hiding its sin from fear of them, but exposing them to view in the most shameless manner. - <hi type="italic">“The look of their faces testifies against them, and their sin they make known like Sodom, without concealing it: woe to their soul! for they do themselves harm.”</hi> In any case, the prophet refers to the impudence with which their enmity against God was shamelessly stamped upon their faces, without even the self-condemnation which leads in other cases to a diligent concealment of the sin. But we cannot follow Luzzatto and Jos. Kimchi, who take <hi type="italic">haccârath</hi> as used directly for <hi type="italic">azzuth</hi> (impudence), inasmuch as the Arabic <hi type="italic">hakara</hi> (<hi type="italic">hakir‛a</hi>), to which Kimchi appeals, signifies to be astonished and to stare (see at <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference>). And in this case there would be nothing strange in the substantive form, which would be a <hi type="italic">piel</hi> formation like בּלּהה חטּאה. But it may be a <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> formation (Ewald, §156, <hi type="italic">a</hi>); and this is incomparably the more probable of the two, as <hi type="italic">hiccir</hi> <hi type="italic">panim</hi> is a very common phrase. It signifies to look earnestly, keenly, or inquiringly in the face of a person, to fix the eye upon him; and, when used of a judge, to take the part of a person, by favouring him unjustly (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deu 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.19">Deu 16:19</reference>). But this latter idea, viz., “their acceptance of the person, or partiality” (according to <reference osisRef="Prov.24.23">Pro 24:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.21">Pro 28:21</reference>), is inadmissible here, for the simple reason that the passage refers to the whole nation, and not particularly to the judges. “The look of their faces” (<hi type="italic">haccârath</hi> <hi type="italic">p'nēhem</hi>) is to be understood in an objective sense, viz., the appearance (τὸ εἶδος, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.29">Luk 9:29</reference>), like the <hi type="italic">agnitio</hi> of Jerome, <hi type="italic">id quo se agnoscendum dat vultus eorum</hi>. This was probably the expression commonly employed in Hebrew for what we designate by a very inappropriate foreign word, viz., physiognomy, i.e., the expression of the face which reveals the state of the mind. This expression of their countenance testified against them (<hi type="italic">anah</hi> <hi type="italic">b'</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.59.12">Isa 59:12</reference>), for it was the disturbed and distorted image of their sin, which not only could not be hidden, but did not even wish to be; in a word, of their <hi type="italic">azzuth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.1">Ecc 8:1</reference>). And it did not even rest with this open though silent display: they spoken openly of their sin (<hi type="italic">higgid</hi> in its simplest meaning, <hi type="italic">palam facere</hi>, from <hi type="italic">nâgad</hi>, <hi type="italic">nagâda</hi>, to be open, evident) without making any secret of it, like the Sodomites, who publicly proclaimed their fleshly lusts (Gen 19). Jerusalem was spiritually Sodom, as the prophet called it in Isa 1:10. By such barefaced sinning they did themselves harm (<hi type="italic">gâmal</hi>, lit., to finish, then to carry out, to show practically).<note placement="foot">It may now be accepted as an established fact, that the verb <hi type="italic">gâmal</hi> is connected with the Arabic <hi type="italic">'gamala</hi>, to collect together, <hi type="italic">'gamula</hi>, to be perfect, <hi type="italic">kamala</hi>, <hi type="italic">kamula</hi> <hi type="italic">id</hi>., and <hi type="italic">gâmar</hi>, to finish (see Hupfeld on <reference osisRef="Ps.7.5">Psa 7:5</reference>, and Fürst, <hi type="italic">Heb. Lex.</hi>).</note>
entries.28799bc6910a8445d4c36cd9bbf59c78f87cd310: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">Isa 3:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen12834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12835" type="x-p"/> The prophet’s meaning is evident enough. But inasmuch as it is the curse of sin to distort the knowledge of what is most obvious and self-evident, and even to take it entirely away, the prophet dwells still longer upon the fact that all sinning is self-destruction and self-murder, placing this general truth against its opposite in a palillogical Johannic way, and calling out to his contemporaries in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Isa 3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">Isa 3:11</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Say of the righteous, that it is well with him; for they will enjoy the fruit of their doings. Woe to the wicked! it is ill; for what his hands have wrought will be done to him.”</hi> We cannot adopt the rendering “Praise the righteous,” proposed by Vitringa and other modern commentators; for although <hi type="italic">âmar</hi> is sometimes construed with the accusative of the object (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">Psa 40:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.6">Psa 145:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.11">Psa 145:11</reference>), it never means to praise, but to declare (even in <reference osisRef="Ps.40.11">Psa 40:11</reference>). We have here what was noticed from <reference osisRef="Gen.1.4">Gen 1:4</reference> onwards - namely, the obvious <hi type="italic">antiptôsis</hi> or <hi type="italic">antiphonêsis</hi> in the verbs ראה (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">Isa 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.2.2">Exo 2:2</reference>), ידע (1Ki 5:17), and אמר (like λέγειν, Joh 9:9): <hi type="italic">dicite justum quod bonus</hi> = <hi type="italic">dicite justum esse bonum</hi> (Ewald, §336, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The object of sight, knowledge, or speech, is first of all mentioned in the most general manner; then follows the qualification, or more precise definition. טוב, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.11">Isa 3:11</reference> רע (רע without the pause), might both of them be the third pers. pret. of the verbs, employed in a neuter sense: the former signifying, it is well, viz., with him (as in <reference osisRef="Deut.5.30">Deu 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.16">Jer 22:15-16</reference>); the latter, it is bad (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.32">Psa 106:32</reference>). But it is evident from <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer 44:17</reference> that הוּא טוב and הוּא רע may be used in the sense of καλῶς (κακῶς) ἔχει, and that the two expressions are here thought of in this way, so that there is no לו to be supplied in either case. The form of the first favours this; and in the second the accentuation fluctuates between אוי <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi> לרשׁע <hi type="italic">munach</hi>, and the former with <hi type="italic">merka</hi>, the latter <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>. At the same time, the latter mode of accentuation, which is favourable to the personal rendering of רע, is supported by editions of some worth, such as Brescia 1494, Pesaro 1516, Venice 1515, 1521, and is justly preferred by Luzzatto and Bär. The summary assertions, The righteous is well, the wicked ill, are both sustained by their eventual fate, in the light of which the previous misfortune of the righteous appears as good fortune, and the previous good fortune of the wicked as misfortune. With an allusion to this great difference in their eventual fate, the word “say,” which belongs to both clauses, summons to an acknowledgment of the good fortune of the one and the misfortune of the other. O that Judah and Jerusalem would acknowledge their to their own salvation before it was too late! For the state of the poor nation was already miserable enough, and very near to destruction.
entries.bce9dd925b6ec6f9df21e607bdb57dad03e5c6b4: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference> <hi type="italic">“My people, its oppressors are boys, and women rule over it; my people, thy leaders are misleaders, who swallow up the way of thy paths.”</hi> It is not probable that <hi type="italic">me‛olel</hi> signifies maltreaters or triflers, by the side of the parallel <hi type="italic">nâshim</hi>; moreover, the idea of despotic treatment is already contained in <hi type="italic">nogesaiv</hi>. We expect to find children where there are women. And this is one meaning of <hi type="italic">me‛olel</hi>. It does not mean a suckling, however, as Ewald supposes (§160, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), more especially as it occurs in connection with <hi type="italic">yonek</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.7">Jer 44:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">Lam 2:11</reference>), and therefore cannot have precisely the same meaning; but, like עולל and עולל (the former of which may be contracted from <hi type="italic">meolēl</hi>), it refers to the boy as playful and wanton (<hi type="italic">Lascivum</hi>, <hi type="italic">protervum</hi>). Böttcher renders it correctly, <hi type="italic">pueri</hi>, <hi type="italic">lusores</hi>, though <hi type="italic">meolēl</hi> is not in itself a collective form, as he supposes; but the singular is used collectively, or perhaps better still, the predicate is intended to apply to every individual included in the plural notion of the subject (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.20.4">Isa 20:4</reference>, and Ges. §146, 4): the oppressors of the people, every one without exception, were (even though advanced in years) mere boys or youths in their mode of thinking and acting, and made all subject to them the football of their capricious humour. Here again the person of the king is allowed to fall into the background. but the female rule, referred to afterwards, points us to the court. And this must really have been the case when Ahaz, a young rake, came to the throne at the age of twenty (according to the lxx twenty-five), possibly towards the close of the reign of Jotham. With the deepest anguish the prophet repeats the expression “my people,” as he passes in his address to his people from the rulers to the preachers: for the <hi type="italic">meassherim</hi> or leaders are prophets (Mic 3:5); but what prophets! Instead of leading the people in a straight path, they lead them astray (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.15">Isa 9:15</reference>, cf., 2Ki 21:9). This they did, as we may gather from the history of this crowd of prophets, either by acting in subservience to the ungodly interests of the court with dynastic or demagogical servility, or by flattering the worst desires of the people. Thus the way of the path of the people, i.e., the highway or road by whose ramifying paths the people were to reach the appointed goal, had been swallowed up by them, i.e., taken away from the sight and feet of the people, so that they could not find it and walk therein (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.25.7-Isa.25.8">Isa 25:7-8</reference>, where the verb is used in another connection). What is swallowed up is invisible, has disappeared, without a grace being left behind. The same idea is applied in <reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference> to a galloping horse, which is said to swallow the road, inasmuch as it leaves piece after piece behind it in its rapid course. It is stated here with regard to the prophets, that they swallow up the road appointed by Jehovah, as the one in which His people were to walk, just as a criminal swallows a piece of paper which bears witness against him, and so hides it in his own stomach. Thus the way of salvation pointed out by the law was no longer to be either heard of or seen. The prophets, who ought to have preached it, said <hi type="italic">mum</hi>, <hi type="italic">mum</hi>, and kept it swallowed. It had completely perished, as it were, in the erroneous preaching of the false prophets.
entries.776c1aec69f52df6ad8614622a1027763d5b35c2: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.13">Isa 3:13</reference> <div eID="gen12835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12836" type="x-p"/> This was how it stood. There was but little to be expected from the exhortations of the prophet; so that he had to come back again and again to the proclamation of judgment. The judgment of the world comes again before his mind. - <hi type="italic">“Jehovah has appeared to plead, and stands up to judge the nations.”</hi> When Jehovah, weary with His long-suffering, rises up from His heavenly throne, this is described as “standing up” (<hi type="italic">kum</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Isa 2:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">Isa 33:10</reference>); and when He assumes the judgment-seat in the sight of all the world, this is called “sitting down” (<hi type="italic">yashab</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.12">Joe 3:12</reference>); when, having come down from heaven (Mic 1:2.), He comes forward as accuser, this is called “standing” (<hi type="italic">nizzab</hi> or <hi type="italic">amad</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Psa 82:1</reference> : <hi type="italic">amad</hi> is coming forward and standing, as the opposite of sitting; <hi type="italic">nizzab</hi>, standing, with the subordinate idea of being firm, resolute, ready). This pleading (<hi type="italic">ribh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.31">Jer 25:31</reference>) is also judging (<hi type="italic">din</hi>), because His accusation, which is incontrovertible, contains the sentence in itself; and His sentence, which executes itself irresistibly, is of itself the infliction of punishment. Thus does he stand in the midst of the nations at once accuser, judge, and executioner (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.8">Psa 7:8</reference>). But among the nations it is more especially against Israel that He contends; and in Israel it is more especially against the leaders of the poor misguided and neglected people that He sets Himself.
entries.4ff8ee893dfc0cdcc065a5c80c89f5704dc7ac94: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.14-Isa.3.15">Isa 3:14-15</reference> <hi type="italic">“Jehovah will proceed to judgment with the elders of His people, and its princes. And ye, ye have eaten up the vineyard; prey of the suffering is in your houses. What mean ye that ye crush my people, and grind the face of the suffering? Thus saith the Lord Jehovah of hosts.”</hi> The words of God Himself commence with <hi type="italic">“and ye”</hi> (<hi type="italic">v'attem</hi>). The sentence to which this (<hi type="italic">et vos</hi> = <hi type="italic">at vos</hi>) is the antithesis is wanting, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>, where the words of God commence with “and I” (<hi type="italic">va'ani</hi>, <hi type="italic">et ego</hi> = <hi type="italic">ast ego</hi>). the tacit clause may easily be supplied, viz., I have set you over my vineyard, but he have consumed the vineyard. The only question is, whether the sentence is to be regarded as suppressed by Jehovah Himself, or by the prophet. Most certainly by Jehovah Himself. The majesty with which He appeared before the rulers of His people as, even without words, a practical and undeniable proof that their majesty was only a shadow of His, and their office His trust. But their office consisted in the fact that Jehovah had committed His people to their care. The vineyard of Jehovah was His people - a self-evident figure, which the prophet dresses up in the form of a parable in chapter 5. Jehovah had appointed them as gardeners and keepers of this vineyard, but they themselves have become the very beasts that they ought to have warded off. בּער is applied to the beasts which completely devour the blades of a corn-field or the grapes of a vineyard (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.4">Exo 22:4</reference>). This change was perfectly obvious. The possessions stolen from their unhappy countrymen, which were still in their houses, were the tangible proof of their plundering of the vineyard. “The suffering:” <hi type="italic">ani</hi> (<hi type="italic">depressus</hi>, the crushed) is introduced as explanatory of <hi type="italic">haccerem</hi>, the prey, because depression and misery were the ordinary fate of the congregation which God called His vineyard. It was <hi type="italic">ecclesia</hi> <hi type="italic">pressa</hi>, but woe to the oppressors! In the question “what mean ye?” (<hi type="italic">mallâcem</hi>) the madness and wickedness of their deeds are implied. מה and לכם are fused into one word here, as if it were a prefix (as in <reference osisRef="Exod.4.2">Exo 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.6">Eze 8:6</reference>; Mal 1:13; vid., Ges. §20, 2). The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> helps to make it clear by resolving the <hi type="italic">chethibh</hi>. The word <hi type="italic">mallâcem</hi> ought, strictly speaking, to be followed by <hi type="italic">chi</hi>: “What is there to you <hi type="italic">that</hi> ye crush my people?” as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.1">Isa 22:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.16">Isa 22:16</reference>; but the words rush forwards (as in <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.6">Jon 1:6</reference>), because they are an explosion of wrath. For this reason the expressions relating to the behaviour of the rulers are the strongest that can possibly be employed. דּכּא (crush) is also to be met with in <reference osisRef="Prov.22.22">Pro 22:22</reference>; but “grind the face” (<hi type="italic">tâchan</hi> <hi type="italic">p'ne</hi>) is a strong metaphor without a parallel. The former signifies “to pound,” the latter “to grind,” as the millstone grinds the corn. They grind the faces of those who are already bowed down, thrusting them back with such unmerciful severity, that they stand as it were annihilated, and their faces become as white as flour, or as the Germans would say, cheese-white, chalk-white, as pale as death, from oppression and despair. Thus the language supplied to a certain extent appropriate figures, with which to describe the conduct of the rulers of Israel; but it contained no words that could exhaust the immeasurable wickedness of their conduct: hence the magnitude of their sin is set before them in the form of a question, “What is to you?” i.e., What indescribable wickedness is this which you are committing? The prophet hears this said by Jehovah, the majestic Judge, whom he here describes as <hi type="italic">Adonai</hi> <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> <hi type="italic">Zebaoth</hi> (according to the Masoretic pointing). This triplex name of God, which we find in the prophetic books, viz., frequently in Amos and also in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jer 2:19</reference>, occurs for the first time in the Elohistic Psalm, Psa 69:7. This scene of judgment is indeed depicted throughout in the colours of the Psalms, and more especially recals the (Elohistic) Psalm of Asaph (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.8">Psa 82:1-8</reference>).
entries.b134068de06d5ee43931bd75ed76b4251fed6019: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16-Isa.3.17">Isa 3:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen12836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12837" type="x-p"/> But notwithstanding the dramatic vividness with which the prophet pictures to himself this scene of judgment, he is obliged to break off at the very beginning of his description, because another word of Jehovah comes upon him. This applies to the women of Jerusalem, whose authority, at the time when Isaiah prophesied, was no less influential than that of their husbands who had forgotten their calling. <hi type="italic">“Jehovah hath spoken: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk about with extended throat, and blinking with the eyes, walk about with tripping gait, and tinkle with their foot-ornaments: the Lord of all makes the crown of the daughters of Zion scabbed, and Jehovah will uncover their shame.”</hi> Their inward pride (<hi type="italic">gâbah</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.50">Eze 16:50</reference>; cf., Zep 3:11) shows itself outwardly. They walk with extended throat, i.e., bending the neck back, trying to make themselves taller than they are, because they think themselves so great.
