The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> substitutes the more usual form, נטוּית; but Isaiah in all probability intentionally made use of the rarer and ruder form <hi type="italic">netuvoth</hi>, since such a form really existed (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">1Sa 25:18</reference>), as well as the singular <hi type="italic">nâtu</hi> for <hi type="italic">nâtui</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.15.22">Job 15:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.41.25">Job 41:25</reference> : Ges. §75, Anm. 5). They also went winking the eyes (<hi type="italic">mesakkeroth</hi>, for which we frequently find the <hi type="italic">erratum</hi> <hi type="italic">mesakkeroth</hi>), i.e., casting voluptuous and amatory glances with affected innocence (νεύματα ὀφθαλμῶν, lxx). <hi type="italic">“Winking:”</hi> <hi type="italic">sâkar</hi> is not used in the sense of <hi type="italic">fucare</hi> (Targ. <hi type="italic">b. Sabbath</hi> 62 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, <hi type="italic">Jome</hi> 9 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, Luther) - which is all the more inappropriate, because blackening the eyelids with powder of antimony was regarded in the East of the Old Testament as indispensable to female beauty - but in the sense of <hi type="italic">nictare</hi> (lxx, Vulg., Syr., <hi type="italic">syn.</hi> <hi type="italic">remaz</hi>, cf., <hi type="italic">sekar</hi>, Syr. to squint; Targ. = <hi type="italic">shâzaph</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.20.9">Job 20:9</reference>). Compare also the <hi type="italic">talmud</hi>ic saying: God did not create woman out of Adam’s ear, that she might be no eavesdropper (<hi type="italic">tsaithânith</hi>), nor out of Adam’s eyes, that she might be no winker (<hi type="italic">sakrânith</hi>).<note placement="foot">Also <hi type="italic">b. Sota</hi> 47b: “Since women have multiplied with extended necks and winking eyes, the number of cases has also multiplied in which it has been necessary to resort to the curse water (Num 5:18).” In fact, this increased to such an extent, that Johanan ben Zakkai, the pupil of Hillel, abolished the ordeal (divine-verdict) of the Sota (the woman suspected of adultery) altogether. The people of his time were altogether an adulterous generation.</note> <div eID="gen12837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12838" type="x-p"/> The third was, that they walked <hi type="italic">incedendo et trepidando</hi>. The second inf. abs. is in this case, as in most others, the one which gives the distinct tone, whilst the other serves to keep before the eye the occurrence indicated in its finite verb (Ges. §131, 3). They walk about tripping (<hi type="italic">tâphop</hi>, a wide-spread onomato-poetic word), i.e., taking short steps, just putting the heel of one foot against the toe of the other (as the <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi> explains it). Luther renders it, “they walk along and waggle” (<hi type="italic">schwânzen</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">Clunibus agitatis</hi>). The rendering is suitable, but incorrect. They could only take short steps, because of the chains by which the costly foot-rings (<hi type="italic">achâsim</hi> ) worn above their ankles were connected together. These chains, which were probably ornamented with bells, as is sometimes the case now in the East, they used to tinkle as they walked: they made an ankle-tinkling with their feet, setting their feet down in such a manner that these ankle-rings knocked against each other. The writing <hi type="italic">beraglēhem</hi> (masc.) for <hi type="italic">beraglēhen</hi> (fem.) is probably not an unintentional <hi type="italic">synallage gen</hi>.: they were not modest <hi type="italic">virgines</hi>, but cold, masculine <hi type="italic">viragines</hi>, so that they themselves were a <hi type="italic">synallage generis</hi>. Nevertheless they tripped along. Tripping is a child’s step. Nevertheless they tripped along. Tripping is a child’s step. Although well versed in sin and old in years, the women of Jerusalem tried to maintain a youthful, childlike appearance. They therefore tripped along with short, childish steps. The women of the Mohammedan East still take pleasure in such coquettish tinklings, although they are forbidden by the Koran, just as the women of Jerusalem did in the days of Isaiah. The attractive influence of natural charms, especially when heightened by luxurious art, is very great; but the prophet is blind to all this splendour, and seeing nothing but the corruption within, foretells to these rich and distinguished women a foul and by no means aesthetic fate. The Sovereign Ruler of all would smite the crown of their head, from which long hair was now flowing, with scab (<hi type="italic">v'sippach</hi>, a progressive preterite with <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> <hi type="italic">apodosis</hi>, a denom. verb from <hi type="italic">sappachath</hi>, the scurf which adheres to the skin: see at <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">Hab 2:15</reference>); and Jehovah would uncover their nakedness, by giving them up to violation and abuse at the hands of coarse and barbarous foes - the greatest possible disgrace in the eyes of a woman, who covers herself as carefully as she can in the presence of any stranger (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Isa 47:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Nah 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.22">Jer 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.37">Eze 16:37</reference>).
entries.ec137cba5dc9b013e49a09aff1aebc01f2252009: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.18-Isa.3.23">Isa 3:18-23</reference> <div eID="gen12838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12839" type="x-p"/> The prophet then proceeds to describe still further how the Lord would take away the whole of their toilet as plunder. <hi type="italic">“On that day the Lord will put away the show of the ankle-clasps, and of the head-bands, and of the crescents; the ear-rings, and the arm-chains, and the light veils; the diadems, and the stepping-chains, and the girdles, and the smelling-bottles, and the amulets; the finger-rings, and the nose-rings; the gala-dresses, and the sleeve-frocks, and the wrappers, and the pockets; the hand-mirrors, and the Sindu-cloths, and the turbans, and the gauze mantles.”</hi> The fullest explanation of all these articles of female attire is to be found in N. W. Schröder’s work, entitled <hi type="italic">Commentarius de vestitu mulierum Hebraearum ad Jes</hi>. <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16-Isa.3.24">Isa 3:16-24</reference>, Ludg. Batav 1745 (a quarto volume), and in that of <hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> Theod. Hartmann, consisting of three octavo volumes, and entitled <hi type="italic">Die Hebräerin am Putztische und als Braut</hi> (The Jewess at the Toilet-table, and as Bride, 1809-10); to which we may also add, Saalschütz, <hi type="italic">Archaeologie</hi>, chapter iii., where he treats of the dresses of men and women. It was not usually Isaiah’s custom to enter into such minute particulars. Of all the prophets, Ezekiel was the one most addicted to this, as we may see, for example, from Ezek 16. And even in other prophecies against the women we find nothing of the kind again (Isa 32:9.; Amo 4:1.). But in this instance, the enumeration of the female ornaments is connected with that of the state props in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1-Isa.3.3">Isa 3:1-3</reference>, and that of the lofty and exalted in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.13-Isa.2.16">Isa 2:13-16</reference>, so as to form a trilogy, and has its own special explanation in that boundless love of ornament which had become prevalent in the time of Uzziah-Jotham. It was the prophet’s intention to produce a ludicrous, but yet serious impression, as to the immeasurable luxury which really existed; and in the prophetic address, his design throughout is to bring out the glaring contrast between the titanic, massive, worldly glory, in all its varied forms, and that true, spiritual, and majestically simple glory, whose reality is manifested from within outwards. In fact, the theme of the whole address is the way of universal judgment leading on from the false glory to the true. The general idea of <hi type="italic">tiphereth</hi> (show: rendered “bravery” in Eng. ver.) which stands at the head and includes the whole, points to the contrast presented by a totally different <hi type="italic">tiphereth</hi> which follows in Isa 4:2. In explaining each particular word, we must be content with what is most necessary, and comparatively the most certain. <hi type="italic">“Ankle-clasps”</hi> (<hi type="italic">acâsim</hi>): these were rings of gold, silver, or ivory, worn round the ankles; hence the denom. verb (<hi type="italic">icces</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa 3:16</reference>, to make a tinkling sound with these rings. <hi type="italic">“Head-bands,”</hi> or <hi type="italic">“frontlets”</hi> (<hi type="italic">shebisim</hi>, from <hi type="italic">shâbas</hi> = <hi type="italic">shâbatz</hi>: <hi type="italic">plectere</hi>), were plaited bands of gold or silver thread worn below the hair-net, and reaching from one ear to the other. There is some force, however, in the explanation which has been very commonly adopted since the time of Schröder, namely, that they were sun-like balls (= <hi type="italic">shemisim</hi>), which were worn as ornaments round the neck, from the Arabic <hi type="italic">‛sumeisa</hi> (<hi type="italic">‛subeisa</hi>), a little sun. The <hi type="italic">“crescents”</hi> (<hi type="italic">saharonim</hi>) were little pendants of this kind, fastened round the neck and hanging down upon the breast (in Jdg 8:21 we meet with them as ornaments hung round the camels’ necks). Such ornaments are still worn by Arabian girls, who generally have several different kinds of them; the <hi type="italic">hilâl</hi>, or new moon, being a symbol of increasing good fortune, and as such the most approved charm against the evil eye. <hi type="italic">“Ear-rings”</hi> (<hi type="italic">netiphoth</hi>, ear-drops): we meet with these in Jdg 8:26, as an ornament worn by Midianitish kings. Hence the Arabic <hi type="italic">munattafe</hi>, a woman adorned with ear-rings. <hi type="italic">“Arm-chains:”</hi> <hi type="italic">sheroth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">shâra</hi>, to twist. According to the Targum, these were chains worn upon the arm, or spangles upon the wrist, answering to the spangles upon the ankles. <hi type="italic">“Fluttering veils”</hi> (<hi type="italic">re'âloth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">râ'al</hi>, to hang loose): these were more expensive than the ordinary veils worn by girls, which were called <hi type="italic">tza'iph</hi>. “Diadems” (<hi type="italic">pe'erim</hi>) are only mentioned in other parts of the Scriptures as being worn by men (e.g., by priests, bride-grooms, or persons of high rank). <hi type="italic">“Stepping-chains:”</hi> <hi type="italic">tze'âdoth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">tze'âdah</hi>, a step; hence the chain worn to shorten and give elegance to the step. <hi type="italic">“Girdles:”</hi> <hi type="italic">kisshurim</hi>, from <hi type="italic">kâshar</hi> (<hi type="italic">Cingere</hi>), dress girdles, such as were worn by brides upon their wedding-day (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.32">Jer 2:32</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.49.18">Isa 49:18</reference>); the word is erroneously rendered hair-pins (<hi type="italic">kalmasmezayyah</hi>) in the Targum. <hi type="italic">“Smelling-bottles:”</hi> <hi type="italic">botte</hi> <hi type="italic">hannephesh</hi>, holders of scent (<hi type="italic">nephesh</hi>, the breath of an aroma). <hi type="italic">“Amulets:”</hi> <hi type="italic">lechashim</hi> (from <hi type="italic">lâchash</hi>, to work by incantations), gems or metal plates with an inscription upon them, which were worn as a protection as well as an ornament. <hi type="italic">“Finger-rings:”</hi> <hi type="italic">tabbâ'oth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">tâba</hi>, to impress or seal, signet-rings worn upon the finger, corresponding to the <hi type="italic">Chothâm</hi> worn by men upon the breast suspended by a cord. <hi type="italic">“Nose-rings”</hi> (<hi type="italic">nizmê</hi> <hi type="italic">hâaph</hi>) were fastened in the central division of the nose, and hung down over the mouth: they have been ornaments in common use in the East from the time of the patriarchs (<reference osisRef="Gen.24.22">Gen 24:22</reference>) down to the present day. <hi type="italic">“Gala-dresses”</hi> (<hi type="italic">machalâtsoth</hi>) are dresses not usually worn, but taken off when at home. <hi type="italic">“Sleeve-frocks”</hi> (<hi type="italic">ma'atâphâh</hi>): the second tunic, worn above the ordinary one, the Roman <hi type="italic">stola</hi>. <hi type="italic">“Wrappers”</hi> (<hi type="italic">mitpâchoth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">tâphach</hi>, <hi type="italic">expandere</hi>), broad cloths wrapped round the body, such as Ruth wore when she crept in to Boaz in her best attire (Rth 3:15). <hi type="italic">“Pockets”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Charitim</hi>) were for holding money (2Ki 5:23), which was generally carried by men in the girdle, or in a purse (<hi type="italic">Cis</hi>). <hi type="italic">“Hand-mirrors”</hi> (<hi type="italic">gilyonim</hi>): the Septuagint renders this διαφανῆ λακωνικὰ, sc. ἱμάτια, Lacedaemonian gauze or transparent dresses, which showed the nakedness rather than concealed it (from <hi type="italic">gâlâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">retegere</hi>); but the better rendering is mirrors with handles, polished metal plates (from <hi type="italic">gâlâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">polire</hi>), as <hi type="italic">gillâyon</hi> is used elsewhere to signify a smooth table. <hi type="italic">“Sindu-cloths”</hi> (<hi type="italic">sedinim</hi>), veils or coverings of the finest linen, viz., of Sindu or Hindu cloth (σινδόνες) - <hi type="italic">Sindu</hi>, the land of Indus, being the earlier name of India.<note placement="foot">The Mishna (<hi type="italic">Kelim</hi> xxiv 13) mentions three different <hi type="italic">sedinin</hi>: night dresses, curtains, and embroidery. The <hi type="italic">sindon</hi> is frequently referred to as a covering wrapped round the person; and in <hi type="italic">b</hi>.<hi type="italic">Menachoth</hi> 41 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, it is stated that the <hi type="italic">sindom</hi> is the summer dress, the <hi type="italic">sarbal</hi> (cloak) the winter dress, which may help to explain <reference osisRef="Mark.14.51">Mar 14:51</reference>-52.</note><hi type="italic">“Turbans”</hi> (<hi type="italic">tseniphoth</hi>, from <hi type="italic">tsânaph</hi>, <hi type="italic">Convolvere</hi>), the head-dress composed of twisted cloths of different colours. <hi type="italic">“Gauze mantles”</hi> (<hi type="italic">redidim</hi>, from <hi type="italic">râdad</hi>, <hi type="italic">extendere</hi>, <hi type="italic">tenuem facere</hi>), delicate veil-like mantles thrown over the rest of the clothes. Stockings and handkerchiefs are not mentioned: the former were first introduced into Hither Asia from Media long after Isaiah’s time, and a Jerusalem lady no more thought of suing the latter than a Grecian or Roman lady did. Even the veil (<hi type="italic">burko</hi>) now commonly worn, which conceals the whole of the face with the exception of the eyes, did not form part of the attire of an Israelitish woman in the olden time.<note placement="foot">Rashi, however, makes a different statement (<hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi> 65 <hi type="italic">a</hi>), viz., that “Israelitish women in Arabia go out with veils which conceal the face, and those in Media with their mantles fastened about the mouth.”</note> <div eID="gen12839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12840" type="x-p"/> The prophet enumerates twenty-one different ornaments: three sevens of a very bad kind, especially for the husbands of these state-dolls. There is no particular order observed in the enumeration, either from head to foot, or from the inner to the outer clothing; but they are arranged as much <hi type="italic">ad libitum</hi> as the dress itself.
entries.5df6ad50093f8adf0e1b2ed14a7a04504fa8782f: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.24">Isa 3:24</reference> <div eID="gen12840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12841" type="x-p"/> When Jehovah took away all this glory, with which the women of Jerusalem were adorned, they would be turned into wretched-looking prisoners, disfigured by ill-treatment and dirt. - <hi type="italic">“And instead of balmy scent there will be mouldiness, and instead of the sash a rope, and instead of artistic ringlets a baldness, and instead of the dress-cloak a frock of sackcloth, branding instead of beauty.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Mouldiness</hi>, or <hi type="italic">mother</hi> (<hi type="italic">mak</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>, the dust of things that have moulded away), with which they would be covered, and which they would be obliged to breathe, would take the place of the <hi type="italic">bosem</hi>, i.e., the scent of the balsam shrub (<hi type="italic">bâsâm</hi>), and of sweet-scented pomade in general; and <hi type="italic">nipâh</hi> that of the beautifully embroidered girdle (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.24">Pro 31:24</reference>). The meaning of this word is neither “a wound,” as the Targums and Talmud render it, nor “rags,” as given by Knobel, ed. 1 (from <hi type="italic">nâkaph</hi>, <hi type="italic">percutere</hi>, <hi type="italic">perforare</hi>), but the <hi type="italic">rope</hi> thrown over them as prisoners (from <hi type="italic">kâphâh</hi> = <hi type="italic">kâvâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">Contorquere</hi>: lxx, Vulg., Syr.).<note placement="foot">Credner (<hi type="italic">Joel</hi>, p. 147) renders the word “tatters,” from <hi type="italic">nâkaph</hi>, to rub in pieces; but the word has no such meaning, whereas the meaning <hi type="italic">vulnus</hi>, lit., <hi type="italic">percussio</hi>, is admissible (see at <reference osisRef="Job.19.26">Job 19:26</reference>), but does not suit the antithesis. Luzzatto connects it with <hi type="italic">n'kaph</hi>, to bind (from which the <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi> derives its name), and understands it as referring to the dressing applied to wounds, to lint into which the girdle was torn. The most plausible derivation is from <hi type="italic">kâphâh</hi>, which is really employed in post-biblical usage to signify not only to congeal and wrinkle, but also to thicken (<hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi> 21 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, <hi type="italic">l'hakpoth</hi>: “Make the wick thicker, that it may burn the brighter”). It is probably radically akin to the Arabic <hi type="italic">nukbe</hi> (explained in Lamachzari as equivalent to the Persian <hi type="italic">mijân - bend</hi>, a girdle), which is apparently used to denote the coarse girdle worn by peasants or by Arab women of the wandering tribes, resembling a rope of goat’s hair, as distinguished from the artistic and costly girdle worn by women of the upper classes in the towns.</note><hi type="italic">Baldness</hi> takes the place of artistic ringlets (מקשׁה מעשׂה, not מעשׂה, so that it is in apposition: cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.30.20">Isa 30:20</reference>; Ges. §113; Ewald, §287, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The reference is not to golden ornaments for the head, as the Sept. rendering gives it, although <hi type="italic">miksheh</hi> is used elsewhere to signify embossed or carved work in metal or wood; but here we are evidently to understand by the “artificial twists” either curls made with the curling-tongs, or the hair plaited and twisted up in knots, which they would be obliged to cut off in accordance with the mourning customs (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Isa 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12">Isa 22:12</reference>), or which would fall off in consequence of grief. A <hi type="italic">frock of sackcloth</hi> (<hi type="italic">machagoreth</hi> <hi type="italic">sak</hi>), i.e., a smock of coarse haircloth worn next to the skin, such as Layard found depicted upon a bas-relief at Kouyunjik, would take the place of the <hi type="italic">pethigil</hi>, i.e., the <hi type="italic">dress-cloak</hi> (either from <hi type="italic">pâthag</hi>, to be wide or full, with the substantive termination <hi type="italic">ı̄l</hi>, or else composed of <hi type="italic">pethi</hi>, breadth, and <hi type="italic">gil</hi>, festive rejoicing); and <hi type="italic">branding</hi> the place of <hi type="italic">beauty</hi>. <hi type="italic">Branding</hi> (<hi type="italic">Ci</hi> = <hi type="italic">Cevi</hi>, from <hi type="italic">Câvâh</hi>, καἰειν), the mark burnt upon the forehead by their conquerors: <hi type="italic">Ci</hi> is a substantive,<note placement="foot">It is so understood in <hi type="italic">b. Sabbath</hi> 62 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, with an allusion to the proverb, “The end of beauty is burning” (viz., inflammation). In Arabia, the application of the <hi type="italic">C ey</hi> with a red-hot iron (<hi type="italic">mikwâh</hi>) plays a very important part in the medical treatment of both man and beast. You meet with many men who have been burned not only on their legs and arms, but in their faces as well, and, as a rule, the finest horses are disfigured by the <hi type="italic">C ey</hi>. - Wetzstein.</note> not a particle, as the Targum and others render it, and as the <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi> might make it appear. There is something very effective in the inverted order of the words in the last clause of the five. In this five-fold reverse would shame and mourning take the place of proud, voluptuous rejoicing.
entries.8b72b7e3971bb59ba3453c872dec63ebd6331b0e: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.25">Isa 3:25</reference> <div eID="gen12841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12842" type="x-p"/> The prophet now passes over to a direct address to Jerusalem itself, since the “daughters of Zion” and the daughter of Zion in her present degenerate condition. The daughter of Zion loses her sons, and consequently the daughters of Zion their husbands. - <hi type="italic">“Thy men will fall by the sword, and thy might in war.”</hi> The plural <hi type="italic">methim</hi> (the singular of which only occurs in the form <hi type="italic">methu</hi>, with the connecting vowel <hi type="italic">ū</hi> as a component part of the proper names) is used as a prose word in the Pentateuch; but in the later literature it is a poetic archaism. <hi type="italic">“Thy might”</hi> is used interchangeably with “thy men,” the possessors of the might being really intended, like <hi type="italic">robur</hi> and <hi type="italic">robora</hi> in Latin (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">Jer 49:35</reference>).
entries.d93e0d893dad594784e4d5234ee3998efb259f99: <reference osisRef="Isa.3.26">Isa 3:26</reference> <div eID="gen12842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12843" type="x-p"/> What the prophet here foretells to the daughter of Zion he sees in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.26">Isa 3:26</reference> fulfilled upon her: <hi type="italic">“Then will her gates lament and mourn, and desolate is she, sits down upon the ground.”</hi> The gates, where the husbands of the daughters of Zion, who have now fallen in war, sued at one time to gather together in such numbers, are turned into a state of desolation, in which they may, as it were, be heard complaining, and seen to mourn (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">Isa 14:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">Jer 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.4">Lam 1:4</reference>); and the daughter of Zion herself is utterly vacated, thoroughly emptied, completely deprived of all her former population; and in this state of the most mournful widowhood or orphanage, brought down from her lofty seat (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">Isa 47:1</reference>) and princely glory (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.18">Jer 13:18</reference>), she sits down upon the ground, just as Judaea is represented as doing upon Roman medals that were struck after the destruction of Jerusalem, where she is introduced as a woman thoroughly broken down, and sitting under a palm-tree in an attitude of despair, with a warrior standing in front of her, the inscription upon the medal being <hi type="italic">Judaea capta</hi>, or <hi type="italic">devicta</hi>. The Septuagint rendering is quite in accordance with the sense, viz., καὶ καταλειφθἠση μόνη καὶ εἰς την̀ γῆν ἐδαφισθήση (cf., <reference osisRef="Luke.19.44">Luk 19:44</reference>), except that תּשׁב is not the second person, but the third, and נקּתה the third pers. pret. <hi type="italic">niph</hi>. for נקּתה - a pausal form which is frequently met with in connection with the smaller distinctive accents, such as <hi type="italic">silluk</hi> and <hi type="italic">athnach</hi> (here it occurs with <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>, as, for example, in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">Amo 3:8</reference>). The clause “sits down upon the ground” is appended ἀσυνδἔτως - a frequent construction in cases where one of two verbs defines the other in a manner which is generally expressed adverbially (vid., <reference osisRef="1Chr.13.2">1Ch 13:2</reference>, and the inverted order of the words in <reference osisRef="Jer.4.5">Jer 4:5</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.12.6">Isa 12:6</reference>): Zion sits upon the earth in a state of utter depopulation.  <chapter eID="Isa.3"/> <div eID="gen12843" type="x-p"/>

entries.feda91cfd8d274d7a2510591481a69a65b9b9418: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.3.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.3.1" sID="gen40757" type="section"/> <div sID="gen40758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">For, behold.</hi> We stated, a little before, that this is the same subject which the Prophet began to treat towards the close of the former chapter; for he warns the Jews that their wealth, however great it may be, will be of no avail to prevent the wrath of God, which, when it has once been kindled, will burn up all their defenses. Hence it follows that they are chargeable with excessive madness, when, in order to drive away their alarm, they heap up their forces, strength, and warlike accoutrements, consultations, armor, abundant supply of provisions, and other resources.<div eID="gen40758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40759" type="x-p"/>The demonstrative particle <foreign xml:lang="he">הנה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">hinneth</hi>,) “behold,” is employed not only to denote certainty, but to express the shortness of time, as if Isaiah caused wicked men to be eye-witnesses of the event; for it frequently happens that they who do not venture openly to ridicule the judgments of God pass them by, as if they did not at all relate to them, or were still at a great distance. “What is that to us?” say they; “Or, if they shall ever happen, why should we be miserable before the time? Will it not be time enough to think of those calamities when they actually befall us?” Since, therefore, wicked men, in order to set at naught the judgments of God, dig for themselves lurking-places of this description, on this account the Prophet presses them more closely and earnestly, that they may not imagine that the hand of God is distant, or vainly expect that it will be relaxed.<div eID="gen40759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40760" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The Lord Jehovah of hosts will take away from Jerusalem</hi>. This is also the reason why he calls God the <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jehovah of Hosts</hi>, that the majesty of God may terrify their drowsy and sluggish minds; for God has no need of titles, but our ignorance and stupidity must be aroused by perceiving his glory. First, the Prophet threatens that the Jews will have the whole produce of the harvest taken from them, so that they will perish through famine. Immediately afterwards he speaks in the same manner about military guards, and all that relates to the good order of the state. Hence we may infer that the Jews boasted of the prosperity which they at that time enjoyed, so as to entertain a foolish belief that they were protected against every danger. But Isaiah threatens that not only the whole country, but Jerusalem herself, which was the invincible fortress of the nation, will be exposed to God’s chastisements; as if he had said, “The wrath of God will not only fall on every part of the body, but will pierce the very heart.”<div eID="gen40760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40761" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The power and the strength. </hi> <note n="49"> <div sID="gen40762" type="x-p"/> “Heb, ‘the support masculine and the support feminine,’ that is, every kind of support, whether great or small, strong or weak. <hi type="italic">Al kenitz,</hi> <hi type="italic">wal kanitzan</hi>; the wild beast, male and female: proverbially applied both to fishing and hunting; that is, I seized the prey, great or little, good or bad. From hence, as Schultens observes, is explained <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.1">Isaiah 3:1</reference>, literally, <hi type="italic">the male and female stay</hi>; that is, the strong and weak, the great and small.” <hi type="italic">Chappelow</hi>, quoted by <hi type="italic">Lowth.</hi><div eID="gen40762" type="x-p"/> </note> As to the words <foreign xml:lang="he">ומשענה משען</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">mashgnen umashgnenah</hi>) which differ only in this respect, that one is in the masculine, and the other in the feminine genders, I have no doubt that the Prophet intended by this change to express more fully the certainty that supports of every kind would be broken; and therefore I have translated them the <hi type="italic">power</hi> and the <hi type="italic">strength</hi> <note n="50"> <div sID="gen40763" type="x-p"/> Calvin has imitated the Hebrew phrase by the rendering <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">vigorem et vim</hi></foreign>; employing two words, of which one is in the masculine and the other in the feminine gender, and both begin with the same letter, while each of them denotes <hi type="italic">strength</hi>. Our English version has imitated the alliteration by <hi type="italic">stay and the staff</hi> — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen40763" type="x-p"/> </note> I do not agree with those interpreters who view it as referring to the persons of men, for it more appropriately denotes all supports, whatever may be their nature.<div eID="gen40761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40764" type="x-p"/>Still it is doubtful whether the Prophet limits it to food, or extends it to all other kinds of support, which he mentions immediately afterwards. But it is natural to suppose that by <foreign xml:lang="he">משען ומשענה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">mashgnen umashgnenah</hi>) is included generally everything that is necessary to sustain the order of the city or of the people; and next that, for the sake of explanation, he enumerates some particulars. The first clause therefore means, “God will take away every help and assistance by which you think that you are upheld, so that nothing whatever may be left to support you.”<div eID="gen40764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40765" type="x-p"/>Next, he adds, what will be their want and nakedness; and he begins, as we have said, with food and nourishment, which hold the first rank in sustaining the life of men. Now there are two ways in which God takes away the <hi type="italic">strength</hi> of bread and water; either when he deprives us of victuals, or when he takes from them the power of nourishing us; for unless God impart to our food a hidden power, the greatest abundance of it that we may possess will do us no good. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.26">Leviticus 26:26</reference>.) Hence in another passage God is said to <hi type="italic">break the staff of bread</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.4.16">Ezekiel 4:16</reference>,) when <hi type="italic">the bakers deliver the bread by weight</hi>, and yet it does not yield satisfaction. And this comparison ought to be carefully observed, in order to inform us that, even though the belly be will filled, we shall always be hungry, there being nothing but the secret blessing of God that can feed or support us.<div eID="gen40765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40766" type="x-p"/>Though the hunger which the Prophet threatens in this passage may be understood to mean that the fields will be unproductive, or, that God will take away from the Jews every kind of food, yet, since the Prophets are generally accustomed to borrow their forms of expression from the law, this interpretation will apply very well. For he might simply have said, “I will take away the bread and wine;” but he expresses something more secret when he speaks of the <hi type="italic">support of bread and water;</hi> as if he had said that, though the people be not reduced to famine, yet God will make them, even while they are rioting in gluttony, to pine with hunger; for when the blessing of God is withdrawn, all its usefulness will vanish away. We may sum it up in this manner, that the people will have no food to strengthen them; either because they will not have bread and water, or, if they have, will derive no advantage from them.<div eID="gen40766" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.3.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen40757" osisID="Isa.3.1" type="section"/>
